newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish ex-communists seek trial of Walesa ally.
newsitem.headline: Polish ex-communists seek trial of Walesa ally.

text.p: Parliamentarians of Poland's ruling ex-communist party moved on Wednesday to put former interior minister Andrzej Milczanowski on trial over spy allegations that forced a prime minister to quit.

PAP news agency said 139 deputies, mostly from the Democratic Left Alliance (SLD), signed a motion which was submitted to parliament's speaker for Milczanowski to be brought before the State Tribunal, a special court for high officials.

Milczanowski was a minister allied to the then-outgoing President Lech Walesa in December 1995 when he told a stunned parliament that the security service had evidence the SLD's prime minister Jozef Oleksy had long informed for Moscow spies.

Oleksy flatly denied the allegations, admitting only to an unwise acquaintance with a Russian diplomat who later proved to be an intelligence officer, but he was forced to resign early last year and was replaced by a fellow SLD member.
Prosecutors later dropped the probe against him saying the security service evidence was inadequate and seriously flawed.
Milczanowski resigned a few days after dropping his parliamentary bombshell, when Walesa handed over power to ex-communist Aleksander Kwasniewski who had won presidential elections.
He and Walesa insist the former interior minister's actions were justified.
"This is an act of political vengeance," Milczanowski told Polish public radio, adding that he was not afraid of going before the tribunal as he had only been doing his duty.
The ex-communists have charged that the original allegations were cooked up by security service agents loyal to Walesa and bent on discrediting his foes the ex-communists.
Walesa has said the truth of the so-called Oleksy affair can only emerge after this year's parliamentary elections give the opposition a larger presence in parliament.
The motion by the ex-communist deputies and some members of the Peasant Party, which is the junior partner in the ruling coalition, levels five charges against Milczanowski.
These include that he neglected his ministerial responsibilities to properly oversee the security service and therefore harmed the interests of the state and of Oleksy.

He is also accused of delay in informing prosecutors about the fact that he suspected a crime, of revealing secret information openly in parliament, of disseminating his suspicions too freely and of sharing secret security service material with the foreign minister of the time.
